title: Environmental records unlock universal quantum computation from thermal decoherence
abstract: At a fixed thermal exposure, the same stabilizer processor can be classically simulable or quantum universal, depending on which environmental records its controller retains. We give an exact computational classification of energy-counting thermal-idle instruments in a quantum processor with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths. The relaxation time $T_1$, homogeneous coherence time $T_2$, and equilibrium excited-state population $p_e$ determine an exact computational boundary at $(1-p_e)T_2/T_1=1$. If every location lies at or below it, branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions give an explicit efficient classical sampler for the adaptive circuit and its full time-resolved exchange record. Above it at a single repeatedly accessible location, a suitable idle duration and no-exchange conditioning supply distillable ancillas and enable universal quantum computation with polynomial overhead. At finite temperature on the resource side, erasing the record at a sufficiently long, unsplit exposure makes the averaged channel stabilizer measure-and-prepare, and even a terminal parity check then yields only simulable branches. Yet at that same exposure, retaining only the bit recording whether any exchange occurred still heralds distillable ancillas, because a thermal round trip restores the parity after its first exchange has already removed the coherence.
summary: This work classifies quantum computation capabilities based on how a processor interacts with a thermal bath while monitoring its environment. It establishes a critical parameter ($\chi$) that dictates whether the system is classically simulable or capable of universal quantum computation. The key finding is that even minimal environmental records can preserve enough quantum information to enable quantum advantage.
main_problem: The paper determines the computational classification (classically simulable vs. quantum universal) of a stabilizer processor coupled to a monitored thermal bath, based on the environmental records retained by its controller.
main_result: Quantum universal computation is possible if the system parameters exceed a critical boundary ($\chi > 0$), even when only retaining minimal environmental records like whether any exchange occurred.
method: The analysis uses exact computational classification based on energy-counting thermal-idle instruments, deriving time-dependent stabilizer margins ($\gamma$) for different readout protocols.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum processor with ideal stabilizer control coupled to independent local Markov baths, undergoing thermal idle periods where energy exchange is monitored.
key_observables: Signed stabilizer margins ($\gamma_q, \gamma_{par}, \gamma_{\emptyset}$), the calibration number ($\chi$), and the computational boundary $\chi=0$.
important_parameters: Relaxation time ($T_1$), homogeneous coherence time ($T_2$), and equilibrium excited-state population ($p_e$).
main_assumptions: Assumes ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths; the analysis compares resource-side records versus the averaged channel.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the computational boundary ($\chi_{\max} \le 0$ vs. $\chi > 0$) and compare the signed stabilizer margins for different readouts (quiet branch vs. terminal parity).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the computational boundary using the ratio $(1-p_e)T_2/T_1$. It then compares the information retained by different readouts (full record, terminal parity, no exchange bit) to show that retaining minimal information can still herald quantum advantage when $\chi > 0$.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative link between the thermodynamics of open quantum systems (thermal decoherence) and the fundamental limits of quantum computation, suggesting that environmental monitoring itself can be a resource.
